---
title: "What you will learn and how to work"
---

Data Analysis in Life Sciences is a five-week introduction to computing and
biological data analysis. We start with
finding a file and end with an analysis that another person can reproduce.
The workflow is meant to carry into later biology practicals, where R replaces
manual spreadsheet calculations and graph preparation.

## What you should become able to do

- Explain files, folders, paths, applications, memory, storage, and processes
  through the practical actions you use every day.
- Organise and inspect lab files with a small set of command-line tools.
- Connect to a supplied remote Linux environment and distinguish its files from
  the files on your laptop.
- Import and check biological measurements in R, calculate derived variables,
  summarise groups, and make labelled plots.
- Interpret mean, variance, SD, and the difference between individual spread
  and uncertainty in an estimate.
- Interpret a guided t-test and a straight-line fit, with attention to
  independent experimental units, units of measurement, and limitations.
- Write and render an R Markdown report from its saved data and code.

No previous file-system, terminal, R, or statistics knowledge is assumed. We will
practise the same actions several times, with gradually less guidance. Later
courses will develop biological theory and bioinformatics tools; this course
does not teach database searching, sequence alignment, or omics analysis.

Prior chemistry courses are not required to understand an exercise. Chemistry
contexts supply all definitions, inputs, constants, units, and calculation
relationships. For example, percentage yield means 100 times the collected mass
divided by a supplied maximum possible mass. Where an exercise offers biological
or organic-laboratory data, choose one route.

## Working through a topic

Use each topic's **Lecture (slides)** for the explanation and worked visual
examples, then open **Exercises** for the complete instructions and
saved output. Slides use the arrow keys or navigation controls; the link in
each deck opens its exercises. Each topic has a quiz with collapsible hints
and answers. Weekly quizzes provide further review.

The numbered lessons follow a five-week progression. The teaching team supplies
the contact timetable separately. Ask for setup support if an installation fails.

The [five-week study plan](study-plan.qmd) lists the weekly work and checkpoints.
Exercises include new questions and datasets to apply what you have learned.
Keep the named outputs and check that you can regenerate them independently.

For most R lessons, a useful working rhythm is:

1. Open the course `.Rproj` and yesterday's source file.
2. Read the biological question and identify what one row represents.
3. Predict a small example, run it, and explain the result.
4. Complete the practical, using hints and references as needed.
5. Save code, a plot or report, and a short interpretation.
6. Close/restart, reopen the work, and check that you can regenerate it.

## Three command interfaces to distinguish

| Interface | Typical commands | What it acts on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local shell in Ubuntu or Mac Terminal | `pwd`, `ls`, `unzip` | Files and programs on your laptop |
| R console in RStudio | `mean()`, `read_csv()`, `ggplot()` | R objects and files accessible to that R session |
| Remote shell after SSH | `pwd`, `ls`, the supported remote commands | Files and programs on the remote computer |

The prompt and window help identify the interface, but always ask which computer
and folder you are using. A folder called `data` does not identify the computer
that holds it.

## What to keep

Preserve the raw data. Save R code or `.Rmd` source, not only a screenshot or
printed number. Keep generated figures and HTML reports with their source and
use the supported backup storage. Most daily exercises name a specific file to
leave with; these are practice outputs, not a grading scheme.

The [downloads page](downloads/index.qmd) supplies datasets and a working report
template. Reports are `.Rmd` files; the course website uses Quarto, which you do
not need to author. We initially render HTML to keep the software setup small.

## Getting help

Record the exact error, the line or chunk that produced it, the relevant
filename, and whether you are local or remote. Check the current folder and
object spelling. Never send passwords, host authentication codes, or private
account details in an error report.
